fields.title: Dispetcher: Nine Requests and One Goal
fields.summary: The backlog is a collection of requests from different people. Decide what you will design this quarter and how.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you design and release this quarter and how will you do it?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Dispetcher, an internal product of the Surma transport company.
fields.brief/company: Surma is a fictional transport company: 60 trucks, long-haul, 74 drivers. Dispetcher is used by eight dispatchers.
fields.brief/context: The Operations Director set a goal for the half-year: reduce empty mileage from 18% to 14%. There are nine items in the backlog, each brought by one of the managers. You have two developers, one designer, and one quarter.
fields.brief/objective: Decide exactly what you will design and release this quarter.
fields.brief/constraints: One quarter, two developers. You will have to say no to most of the requesters.
fields.brief/task: Choose an approach and justify what will make it into the quarter and why.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A backlog is just a list of requests until it is linked to behavior
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Nine items from nine respected people look identical until you build a chain for each: goal → who influences it → what behavior needs to change. Once you do this, the debate usually ends on its own. And you should design what survives starting with objects and states: a screen that the system cannot populate costs more than a week of conversations at the start.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
1. Downtime dashboard—Operations Director.
2. Return trip suggestion during planning—dispatcher Natalya.
3. Export to 1C—accounting.
4. Mobile side cargo request for drivers—fleet manager.
5. Visibility of available return legs a week ahead—sales department.
6. Dark theme—two dispatchers.
7. Push notifications for drivers—fleet manager.
8. Vehicle directory refactoring—development, 'tech debt there'.
9. Dispatcher-to-driver chat—Operations Director.

Development estimates: 2—three weeks, 4—five weeks, 5—two weeks, 1—one week, 6—three days, 3—two weeks.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
You spent two mornings sitting next to Natalya.

Trip planning: she opens the order list, selects an order, finds a truck, and assigns a driver. The system never asks about a return load—this step is completely missing from the flow.

She looks for return orders in a separate tab sorted by creation date, matching cities manually using a map on the wall.

Twice in two mornings, she selected an order that another dispatcher had taken just a minute earlier. The system only reported this after confirmation, forcing her to cancel and rebuild the trip.

When asked what would be most useful, Natalya replied: 'A chat with drivers, because right now I have to call them.' She said nothing about return legs—it is not perceived as a product task.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: How the system is set up now
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The 'trip' object has states: draft, planned, assigned to driver, en route, completed.

Cancellation after departure cannot be represented in the system: the dispatcher changes the trip to 'completed' and creates a new one. The remaining cargo is not stored anywhere.

There is no 'leg' object (a route segment between two points) in the system—only the trip as a whole. Consequently, a return trip cannot be linked to the outbound trip.

An order is not locked while a truck is being assigned: two dispatchers can work on the same order simultaneously.

A driver in the system is just an employee with a category; side cargo does not exist as an object.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Build the chain to the goal and start with objects
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Link the backlog to the goal through behavior, keep the paths that actually move the needle, and design them starting with objects and flows rather than screens.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Creating an impact map takes half a day and cuts six out of nine items: neither the dashboard, the chat, nor the export change anyone's behavior toward the goal.
What remains is the return trip suggestion (61% of losses), return leg visibility for sales (22%), and side cargo requests (legalizes 40 trips that previously went off the books).
When analyzing objects, the main issue emerges: there is no 'leg' object in the system, and without it, return trip suggestions are physically impossible to build. This is two weeks of work no one knew about—and it is discovered before the start, not in the middle of the quarter.
In the flow, the conflict between two dispatchers over an order surfaces: a lock is added in two days because it is in the same piece of code.
The quarter fits leg + suggestion + lock. Empty mileage for the quarter drops from 18% to 16.2%.
Compromise: the Operations Director asked about his dashboard twice, and you had to explain the rejection in person.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Build the downtime dashboard and chat
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Both items were requested by the Operations Director, who also set the goal. Build what the stakeholder asks for.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The dashboard is released in three weeks, the chat in six.
The dashboard shows the same 18% as the spreadsheet export, just daily now. It doesn't change decisions: dispatchers still plan trips without thinking about return loads because this step is missing from the flow.
The chat is used eagerly—it is indeed more convenient than calls. It has zero impact on empty mileage.
At the end of the quarter, empty mileage is at 17.8%. The director asks why the goal isn't moving, and you don't have a good answer: you did exactly what he asked.
Compromise: you fulfilled requests instead of solving the problem; you have no arguments left to defend your approach because you didn't gather any data.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Hand over mockups of all screens to the designer
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The fastest way is to show people what it will look like. The designer draws the return trip suggestion screens, the design is unified, and then development starts.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Two weeks later, you have beautiful mockups of the return trip suggestion.
During planning, development asks where to get the return leg, and it turns out there is no 'leg' object in the system. The mockups show something the system cannot do.
Refactoring takes another three weeks, including a week to redo those same mockups.
By the end of the quarter, the suggestion feature is released in a stripped-down version, order locking was not built in time, and empty mileage is at 17.4%.
Compromise: the work was done in the wrong order; you got the same result but spent an extra month, and part of the team believes development is to blame.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Take the cheapest items from the backlog
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Dark theme—three days, side cargo request—one week, export to 1C—two weeks. Three happy groups in a quarter and plenty of time to spare.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
All three are released by mid-quarter, and no one has any complaints.
The side cargo request turns out to be a lucky break: 60 trips go through it over the quarter instead of the previous 40 off-the-books ones, and empty mileage drops to 17.6%.
Dark theme and export move nothing.
The team spends the remaining half of the quarter on the vehicle directory tech debt because the roadmap ended.
At the half-year review, the 14% goal looks unreachable, and the discussion is about how the quarter was wasted.
Compromise: low cost was chosen as the criterion instead of alignment with the goal; one hit out of three is luck, not a method.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The feature is described in isolation, without the pain point and the benefit on the other side
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The chain from goal to behavior is incomplete, making it unclear why this needs to be built
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Objects and their states were not defined before designing the screens
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The flow is only designed for the happy path: empty states, errors, and conflicts are ignored
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Consistency and interface copy are mistaken for mere cosmetics
